doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Flat artist deal, recording costs and top royalty
summary: Mitch Miller raised him to the five percent top royalty; Conniff explains recording budgets then and now and that selling product gets a good deal.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: would come out. I never worried about what was in the contract. So it finally got up where I got — I was what they called in those days a flat artist. In other words, I used to go in, they’d pay the cost of my musicians and singers, which was a big item you know — well in those days it wasn’t that big, now it is — it was like, if you’re talking numbers, an album, a total album, musicians and singers, the first albums I did in 1956 I would say maybe $15,000, $12 or $15,000.

Now, musicians and singers, and I’m really, I go in with a time schedule and a budget. You know, I know what I’m doing. I don’t go in there and spend four days on the bass drum you know, like some of the younger artists do, which is all right, they’re selling more records that I am, I’m not knocking it you know. But I would go in and I could do four tunes a session, and I had it all worked out. But now, even working on a tight budget, I’d say a good hundred thousand dollars at least, for musicians and singers. And maybe you can get the cover in there too, the artwork on the CD. But that was in those days, ten or twelve, fifteen, thirteen thousand. But anyway, they paid all of that, and I got the three percent above that. But anyway they got me up then what was called the top royalty, five percent. And they had two different kinds of contracts. Some of the contracts were on wholesale. We’re getting too complicated. Some were wholesale, some were retail. But I had the best I could get at the time. Yeah. To answer you really, the quick answer to the question is, when you’re selling product, you get a good deal. When you’re not selling, it’s tough to get the top deal.
Three percent of nothing isn’t very good.
